rows.title: Policy
rows.figure: Fed held 3.75–4.00% Oct 28 (10–2), Dec hike ~78% (CME via Reuters, from ~84%); BoC 2.50%, Dec ~45%; RBNZ 2.75%; ECB Oct 29 hold ~95%, Dec hike ~89%; BoJ Oct 30 hold ~98%; RBA Nov 3 hike ~79–85%; BoE Nov 5 hike ~94%
rows.read: Most central banks are still leaning toward higher rates because of energy-driven inflation. Markets eased their bets on a December Fed hike a little after chair Kevin Warsh refused to commit, which keeps the dollar steady rather than stronger. The European Central Bank today and the Bank of Japan overnight are both expected to wait until December.

rows.title: Growth
rows.figure: US Q3 GDP today 7:30 AM CT fc 3.0% annualised; Fed: activity 'strong'; Japan consumer confidence 35.0 (fc 35.1); NZ ANZ business confidence 52.5 (from 51.9); Alphabet ~-9% after hours
rows.read: The US economy still looks stronger than Europe's or Britain's, and that gap keeps favouring the dollar. Overnight surveys were mixed: Japanese households a little gloomier, New Zealand firms a little brighter. US third-quarter growth figures this morning are the next big check.

rows.title: Inflation
rows.figure: US core PCE (Sep) today fc +0.3% m/m; Australia Q3 import prices -1.1% q/q (fc +1.8%); NZ firms' pricing plans highest since May; Tokyo CPI tonight 6:30 PM CT fc 2.6%; euro-area CPI 3.8%
rows.read: Energy keeps prices high, which is why most central banks are still leaning toward hikes. There are early signs of relief: Australia's import costs fell as fuel shipping eased. The US inflation measure the Fed watches most comes this morning, and it will shape how sure markets are of a December Fed hike.

rows.title: Risk
rows.figure: Alphabet ~-9% after hours; Kospi -2.8%, Nikkei flat; USD/JPY ~157.75; USD/CHF ~0.828; Vance letter to Iran (WSJ); Trump threatens strikes after midterms
rows.read: Asian shares slipped after a weak result from Google's owner, Alphabet, but there was no rush into safe currencies like the yen and franc. A report of US outreach to Iran eased war fears a little, while threats of strikes after next week's US elections keep the risk alive. Calm for now, but fragile.

rows.figure: Brent ~$114.10 (-1.1%), WTI ~$101.45 (-1.3%, Reuters 03:51 GMT); Houthi refinery strike claim unconfirmed; EIA crude -1.9M bbl; OPEC+ meets Sunday
rows.read: Oil eased on hopes that the US and Iran might talk, but it is still far above pre-war levels. That keeps helping exporters like Canada and Australia and costing importers like Japan and the euro area. A real peace deal would shift that balance quickly.

rows.figure: CFTC Oct 20: funds strongly against CAD (sharply added), against NZD (sharply added) and EUR (added), for GBP (real money strongly against), for AUD (real money strongly against), leaning against JPY, strongly for gold
rows.read: Hedge funds hold their biggest bets against the Canadian dollar, and Canada's rate hike has not yet forced them to buy back. Their bets against the kiwi paid off after New Zealand's surprise hold. In the pound and the Aussie, hedge funds and long-term investors take opposite sides.

rows.title: Fiscal
rows.figure: UK Budget: borrowing 4.2% of GDP this year to 1.8% by 2030–31; headroom £15bn (from £24bn); 10-year gilt yield −2bp; French revenue vote Nov 3; France–Germany 10-year gap ~162–177bp
rows.read: Chancellor John Healey's first UK Budget passed calmly, with borrowing set to fall, so UK bonds and the pound took it in stride. France's budget fight is still unresolved and keeps a weight on the euro; reporters are likely to raise it at the European Central Bank's press conference today.
